title: The Satipatthana, alone
tomorrow: should you steer your breath, or only watch it?

lines: IT LOOKS LIKE A COPYING MISTAKE.
THE SAME LINES, AGAIN AND AGAIN.
cards: A song can have twelve verses and one chorus, and the chorus is what you're humming at the bus stop. Read MN 10 straight through with nobody explaining it, and you hit something that looks like a copying mistake.
Breathing. Then walking, standing, sitting, lying down. The parts of the body.
Feelings. The mind. And after every single section, the same block of lines, word for word, again and again.
Why would a sutta repeat itself like that?

teach.b: Here's the answer: the repeated lines aren't filler. They're the practice. The sections change what you look at; the refrain tells you how to look.
In paraphrase: you stay with the body as body, inside and outside.
You see it arising, and you see it passing. Mindfulness is simply there, just enough to know and keep knowing. And you rest, not leaning on anything, not grabbing at anything in the world.
Then the next section starts, and the refrain comes back for feelings, for the mind, for the teachings themselves.
Same how, new what. That's why reading alone matters. With a guide, the refrain is easy to skip.
Alone, it keeps landing until you notice it's the point.
The sutta opens by calling these four, body, feelings, mind and the teachings, ekayano maggo.
English has put that more than one way: a path that goes one way, a direct path. Whichever word you choose, it means no detour. You don't have to get somewhere else first.
Whatever is here is already the object.

how: The Satipatthana Sutta is a foundation for mindfulness practice in Theravada communities; some teachers have students work through one section at a time, returning to the refrain for each.

o: the sutta on establishing mindfulness in four places
the rules for how monks walk, stand and sit
a set of breathing drills for falling asleep faster

s: the repeated lines in MN 10 are a copying mistake
they're the practice itself: the same way of looking, applied to each new object.
MN 10 covers body, feelings, mind and the teachings
four places to establish mindfulness, each with the same refrain.
mindfulness in MN 10 means emptying the mind of thoughts
the mind itself is one of the things you watch, arising and passing.

games.q: you're dreading a hard conversation tonight and can't focus on homework. what does MN 10 point you to?
o: make the dread itself the object: feel it, see it rise and pass
push the dread away first, then start the real practice
wait until the conversation is over to try again
games.why: the direct path means no detour: feelings and the mind are already objects in the sutta. whatever is here is where it starts.

practice: Try the section on feelings. Each time something registers, a sound, an ache, a thought, notice only its tone: pleasant, unpleasant, or neither. Then watch that tone arise and pass, without leaning toward it or away.

wordCard.voice: The Satipatthana: the sutta on the establishing of mindfulness, MN 10, four places to stand and one refrain for how to look.

orig.note: Pali: the establishing of mindfulness (sati). MN 10 is named for it.

carryVoice: The direct path: no detour, and what's here is enough to start. Sutta one, read alone.
